Then, the paper quotes the question and answer that I have just read from the ' Hansard,' and goes on :
Are you satisfied, Mr. Ingram, that there has been no stupendous jobbery?
I never charged any stupendous jobbery in the matter of the salary of Mr. O'Donoghue, neither do I now.
All right. Now continue your investigations through the whole service, and if you inquire, laying aside party spectacles, you may find a richer haul than the man appointed to see bare justice done to workmen when the public is spending its own money. A workingman who possesses the confidence of his class, and has thus compelled the recognition of the government. We are not denying the right of Mr. Ingram to seek the information in the way ho chooses, but he could have got it all in five minutes by referring to the proper department or the records of last session. If it was a swipe at the O'Donoghue, well, it failed.
It was not a swipe, and it did not fail. What was the object of this purely independent paper ? What is there wrong about making the inquiries that I did ? 1 was quite within my right, and I was justified in making inquiries concerning that gentleman. because the history and pedigree of that gentleman for years past have not been in the interest of the workingmen of this country. He has been a stool pigeon for the Ontario government for years. He lias never missed an opportunity of pulling the chestnuts out of the fire for the government of the province of Ontario. He has been associated with the Trades and Labour Council of the city of Toronto, and he has never missed an opportunity to stab the Conservative party in that province, nor in the Dominion either, for the purposes of party gain. I go further than that. I have been associated with the labour interests in this country. I have been nominated by the Conservative party in every instance, and ever since I have been a member of this House, whenever I could say a word on behalf of the workingmen. I have never neglected to do so, irrespective of party. 1 have reserved the right as a Conservative
to support my party, and I intend to support my party as long as I believe they advocate Conservative principles. But, in doing so, I do not see how I am precluded from supporting the interests of the workingmen of this Canada. While taking that right to myself, I grant the same right to the member for Winnipeg, to the member for Vancouver (Mr. Smith), or any other gentleman in this House. But, when they rise in their places in this House and say to members on both sides : We are independent of both parties, both parties are wrong, and we are right, while at the same time never missing an opportunity to drive water to the Grit mill. I strongly object to that course of procedure. I do not complain because they drive water to the mill of lion, gentlemen opposite, but I complain because they sail under false colours. They are just as much party men as I am. the only difference being that I stand up openly for" my party, while they pretend to stand up as the independent party in this House. That is the difference between the hon. gentlemen and myself.
Now. with respect to the Labour Department, I have no fault to find with its establishment. I believe it will be able to accomplish a good deal of good. With regard to the conciliation Act, I believe it is a step in the right direction, and I said at the time the Act was passed in this House that it was a step in the right direction. But. what I find fault with is the way it is run. When hon. gentlemen on either side of this House stand up in their places and advocate and assist any measure in favour of labour legislation, if they do it in behalf of the principle on which the Act was based, then, that department should miss no opportunity of giving credit to hon. gentlemen on the government side or hon. gentlemen on this side, for the part they take in promoting labour legislation. But. when I look over the Labour Gazette, I find the names of certain gentlemen mentioned who have taken an active part in promoting labour legislation, and 1 know as a matter of fact, that these very same gentlemen have not uttered one word to ten words uttered by other hon. gentlemen in this House whose names are not mentioned at all. I say if that is the way the Labour Department is run. then, we have just reason to find fault with it. I take this stand, that we have already causes enough of division on ordinary party questions ; but, when a question comes up that we believe to be in the interest of labour, then. I think we can fairly consider it as a non-party question, and as members on both sides, we can discuss questions of that character freely and independently of party politics altogether. So. I want my independent friends in this House to understand that, so far as I am concerned. I am just as much in favour of promoting the interests of the workingmen as they are. and

being a Conservative, I see no reason wliy I cannot support my party on purely party questions the same as any Liberal member of this House, or the same as my lion, friends who call themselves independent members.
Having said that much with respect to the O'Donoghue case, having found, during my election, that he was very eager to secure party support for the Liberal candidate who opposed me, I think it is right that I should inquire what are his duties. I know that he consulted some parties there, and he told them that it would be to their interests to support my opponent. Well, if that is to be the business of the man whose duties are supposed to be entirely restricted to finding out the current rate of wages of workingmen employed on public works, I think the sooner this country understands it the better. We have a right to demand that he shall confine his duties to the office to which he was appointed, and to that office alone. I want further to say this. The government may have a reasonable expectation of being in power for some time, but the day will come when the parties in this House will change places, and what is good for them now may be equally good for them when the parties change places. So, I say that gentlemen like Mr. O'Dono-ghue should be given to understand that he had better pay strict attention to his duties for which he is paid, and not interfere with party politics at all. That is all I wish to say on this question. I would be glad to find out from the editor of this paper, who professes to be an independent man in this House, if he finds any fault with the question I asked, or any reason why that item should be placed there for the purpose of making a little party capital ?

I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) who has just taken his seat, is very sensitive on this question. He complains of being attacked. I would like to know where he was attacked. He has quoted from a paper published in the city of Winnipeg, with which I happen to be connected. If he reads the dates he will see that this issue appears since the session opened. I have read the article and that is about all the connection that I have had with it. But, it seems to me that it is only a fair comment. The hon. gentleman, who is apt to be a little inquisitive, asked his question at the time, in order to create a feeling of suspicion in the country, to show that he wanted, especially in connection with this fair-wage officer. to try to place some blame upon Hie party that put hint into office. The article, I think, is fair. I do not write such articles as that myself, but I have no hesitation in fathering this one as far as my connection with the paper is concerned. I think all the hon. gentleman wanted was a chance to attack me, and therefore he

told us what his idea of independence is, and showed that his idea fits his own purpose. His language, I think, is not worthy of the labour people of the country. He has a perfect right to his opinion, if he thinks by such language lie can do service to the party with which he is affiliated. I do not think the same way as he does, but I deny the right of the hon. gentleman to in any way reflect upon my standing in this House. I am here as an independent, elected by the labour people of Winnipeg. 1 come here as an independent labour man. I am not here jas a result of soliciting votes at the expense of any or either of the parties, as I have no party affiliations or leanings whatever. I do not believe in the system of party government as it has been developed in this country, and I have nothing Whatever to do with it. I am here, as far as party is concerned, with hopes and without fears. The hon. member for Elgin has had more experience than I have had in this House. He may know some of the difficulties that a new member and a young man like myself experiences, but my record is here and on that record it is beyond him to criticise me. I have always acted, spoken and voted in this House strictly as an independent labour man, and I deny the hon. gentleman the right, on my record, to contradict that statement. I think he only-wanted an opportunity, by claiming that he had been attacked unfairly in this publication, to attack me on this ground. I have noticed that whenever an hon. gentleman gets up in this House who is not a straight hidebound party man, the hou. member for East Elgin attempts to criticise him and to cast a slur on his independence. He is entitled to any regard he has for his own party, or for the opposite party. I say there is a legitimate and proper field for independence. and there is a field in this House, as far as I can see it. As far as the Labour Bureau is concerned, I want to say, and I say it frankly, that, Tip to the present time,
I have seen very little indication of party influence or tactics there. If the bureau of labour is going to be worked for party [DOT]purposes, I am going to oppose it right through. But, at all events, whatever maybe the other failings of the labour men in this House, theyr voted for the establishment of the Labour Bureau, and for the passage of the fair-wage clause. I believe this is one of those things that we should look after, that we should collect these statistics and look into these labour matters the same as we do into matters connected with any other department of government.

As the Department of Labour is a new department, established only a few months ago, I desire to

give to tlie House some information concerning it, so tlmt lion, gentlemen may know something of its organization and the work which the department has already accomplished. I am sure this information will be of great interest. The Act establishing the Department of Labour was not assented to until the 18th of July last, and on the 15th of September the first number of the Labour Gazette, which is the journal of the department, appeared.
Since that date copies of the Labour Gazette have appeared regularly each month, and a perusal of them will show the extensive work which the new department has already undertaken and performed. The numbers of the Labour Gazette show that the department has undertaken in a systematic way the gathering of information of first importance to employers and employed, on industrial and labour conditions in this country.
Of the special classes of work thus undertaken the following among others may be mentioned
1.	A compendium of labour legislation in the Dominion.
2.	An account of the present extent and development, together with existing conditions, of the different industries of the country.
3.	Statistical tables of the rates of wages and hours of employment in the various trades.
4.	Legal decisions of the various courts in the provinces on matters of concern to labour.
In some of the Labour Bureaus in the United States and in other countries each of these conditions has been dealt with but only in special reports prepared by the bureaus or departments, but the method adopted by the Canadian department in dividing the work into separate articles appearing each month, seems a more useful method and more likely to secure the information thus presented being brought within reach of those persons to whom it is of primary concern. There has never been in Canada before a descriptive and statistical work of this nature undertaken, and in a country covering so wide an area, and with conditions so varying, it is impossible to overrate its importance. Exact knowledge of industrial conditions is most essen tial for any right legislation and such information can only be obtained by some special agency which has opportunity and facilities for collecting it over a considerable period of time. [DOT]
In addition to its historical worth the information so obtained is of very great practical value in acquainting manufacturers as well as workingmen with the condi tion of the labour market and industrial conditions generally in all parts of the Dominion, and, in this connection, the work of the department, in publishing reports every month from special correspondents in
every city of the Dominion, cannot be overestimated. The Labour Gazette has averaged a little over fifty pages each issue and the eight numbers already published would, if bound, give a volume of 456 pages of original material in reference to industrial conditions in Canada. This is one part of the work which the new department has already achieved.
The department lias also achieved important results in connection with the work of conciliation and the settlement of industrial disputes. Four very important disputes have been summarily ended almost immediately after the friendly offices of the department were requested. The strike of the mill operatives in YaUeyfleld, of the coremakers in Oshawa and the tool workers in Dundas are here referred to, and the recent strike at the mills of the Laurentide Pulp Company, Grand Mere, Quebec. Full particulars regarding each will be found in the current numbers of the Gazette. But important as has been the work of conciliation there is no doubt but that the plau adopted by the department in publishing i monthly record of all trade disputes in the Dominion, has aided materially in preventing certain strikes in the first place and in bringing to a close some which had already commenced. The mere fact that an official record is given monthly on this head, and that both parties to a dispute are communicated with by a branch of the government for a statement of their case for publication, has, without question, a good moral effect in preserving industrial peace.
The tables of strikes and lock-outs which appear monthly in the Gazette are of themselves very typical of the importance of the work which the department is doing. These tables classify all of the strikes and lockouts according to the localities in which they occur, the causes, results, duration, numbers affected, &c., and these monthly tables are intended as a basis of an annual report on the subject of trade disputes. Where legislation, for example, such as that of compulsory arbitration, is being considered, exact information as to the nature of the strikes and lock-outs which have occurred, their number, causes, &c„ will be invaluable.
The department has also aided materially in the effective enforcement of the Alien Labour law. There have been but one or two eases of aliens having been deported before the department undertook, by its special officers, to see to the enforcement of this branch of labour legislation. As a result of these efforts no less than fifty-four complaints have been made the subject of special investigation during the months from August to March inclusive, and over 60 persons were deported, or returned to the States, as a result of the action of the department, and there is every reason to believe that a knowledge of the fact that the law was being rigorously enforced has de-

terred many persons from running the risk of violation of its provisions.
Tlie department lias also, through its fair-wages officers seen to the effective carrying out of the resolution adopted in the House of Commons last year to the effect that in all government contracts clauses should' be inserted which would secure the payment of fair wages and the performance of the work under fair conditions wherever it was being performed under contracts for the government, or by private parties aided by grants from the government. A very large number of fair-wage schedules have been prepared in connection with the contracts of the Public Works Department and of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, the Post Office Department and others, and these have been published from month to month in the Labour Gazette so that the public as well as the contractors might be aware of the conditions under which the work was to be performed. Cases where the contractor was not paying the stipulated rate have been brought to the notice of the department and it has caused the sanm to be made the subject of special investigation, and reports thereon have been furnished to the department of the government whose contracts were alleged to have been violated in this particular.
The department has also undertaken the work of collecting statistical and other public information from all possible sources In the Dominion, from which it is intended to form a library and archives having to do with the industrial conditions, of the country and for labour in particular. Supplementary to this is the work of collecting reports and other information from the bureaus of foreign countries in regard to labour. In addition to the work of collecting statistics and disseminating information, which is the chief work of the department, the importance to the working classes of having a readier means of making known then-needs and desires to the government is not to be overlooked.
The Gazette, amongst other statistical material which appears from month to month, gives an account of the numbers employed iu different industries and trades, opportunities for employment, current rates of wages, prices of commodities, etc., all of which is of immediate concern to the working classes and employers, and also to the general industrial condition of the country. The information is not only of present value but of great historical worth and is also helpful in bringing before persons in other lines the industrial development of this country. Thus far the lumbering industry, the coal industry, iron industry, copper and nickel industry and fishing industry have been the subject of special investigation.
The department has begun a comprehen-[DOT]sfve review of the rates of wages and hours of employment obtaining in different trades Mr. SUTHERLAND (Oxford).
in the Dominion. Information from all parts of Canada has been gathered for the different classes of labour employed in the trades dealt with, showing thq rates which are given and the variations between different localities. Thus far the printing trade, the cigar-making trade, and the metal trades have been dealt with. The building trades and others will follow and be published in subsequent numbers of the Gazette.
The department has undertaken a comprehensive review of labour legislation in all parts of the Dominion, dealing with the subject historically and giving a careful classification and compilation of the various Acts at the present time affecting labour. The work when finished will be a complete compendium of labour legislation in Canada and may be used as a work of reference by all persons who desire to have an exact-knowledge of legislation on any point which concerns labour. The information so gathered has also the advantage of presenting a comparative statement of the differences and similarities existing between the legislation of the different provinces. Thus far the legislation in regard to factories, workshops and mines has been fully dealt with.
The department publishes each month a record of all the most important legal decisions in all the provinces of the Dominion which affect in any way either employers or employed.
From month to month a review is given of the most important reports made by public departments in this and other countries on matters affecting labour, and in this manner the public is kept informed of the latest statistical information in the different parts of their own country, and in other lands.
The department publishes each month a record of the most important trade disputes in the Dominion. These are carefully classified and compiled and tables indicating the causes and results of these disputes, their duration and the numbers affected by them are given. This information, as already stated, is of extreme value in furnishing a basis for legislation in regard to the matters of strikes and lockouts.
The plan adopted by the department is : whenever a strike or lock-out occurs in any part of the Dominion, to immediately communicate with both parties to the dispute asking for a, statement of their case for publication in the Gazette. It is believed that in addition to the value of the information so supplied, the knowledge that the department is thus publishing this information and the fact that it so promptly communicates with both parties, has a great moral effect in inducing employers and workmen to come to an immediate settlement of their difficulties.
The department has correspondents in practically all of the cities of the Dominion, and these furnish monthly returns on the

general state of the labour market and conditions of industry and labour in tlieir locality. These appearing every month in the Labour Gazette, give a clear conception of the labour market in this country and enable workmen, as well as employers, to ascertain exact information as to the conditions of the labour market in all parts with which they are immediately concerned. This information, in addition to its present value, will be of extreme worth as time goes on in tracing the industrial growth and development of this country.
I have already alluded to the very considerable results achieved by the department in the work of conciliation during the short time it has been in existence. In the case of three important industrial disputes in which appeals were made to the department from one of the parties for its friendly intervention under the Conciliation Act, a settlement has been effected which has ended the dispute. Each of these cases has been very important, and but for the intervention of the department much suffering and loss would doubtless have followed on the continuance of the existing difficulties.
The'first case was that of the strike of mill operatives at Valleyfield, Que., which took place because of the militia having been sent to that town. Within twenty-four hours after the arrival of the representative of the government, an agreement had taken effect whereby the operatives returned to work and the troops were withdrawn.
The second case was that of the coremakes in the Malleable Iron Works in Osliawa. An appeal was mado to the department by the mayor of the town on behalf of the workingmen, and the immediate intervention of the department resulted in an agreement being effected within twenty-four hours after the arrival of the representative of the government, whereby the grievances which the strikers complained of were adjusted and employment was resumed in the company's works as before. But for this immediate settlement, large numbers might have been thrown out of employment and great suffering experienced during the .winter season.
The third case was that of a long standing dispute between the Bertram Tool Works in Dundas and certain of their employees. This dispute had been in continuance from October of last year, and the intervention of the department was asked in January. A similar result followed on the intervention of the department. A satisfactory agreement between the two parties was effected and the dispute declared to be at an end.
Another case occurred within the past week-that of the strike of the employees of the Laurentide Pulp Mills at Grand M8re, in the province of Quebec. The premier received a telegram from a representative of the workingmen there, some 800 of whom had gone out on strike ; and at their
request I at once telegraphed to the manager of the company and also to the representative of the workingmen, informing them that a representative of the department would be sent down. That was done, with the result that within less than twenty-four hours an amicable arrangement was made, as I am informed, to the great satisfaction of both the men and the company, and all the men returned to work.
These are the only cases in which appeals have been made to the department for intervention under the Act, save in two cases which are at the present time pending, and the result in each case goes to show the effectiveness of voluntary conciliation as a means of adjusting industrial difficulties.
An important work of the department has been to gather all public information in regard to matters affecting labour in this country. This is the first time that any attempt has been made to have these documents collected and filed in such a manner that they may be of service to persons desiring exact information upon conditions either affecting the past or the present. Records of trade unions, friendly societies, &c., are being collected, classified and filed in the department and the basis has already been laid for national archives on matters pertaining to labour. The department has also gathered from other countries statistical reports and general public information in regard to industrial conditions and methods prevailing elsewhere, which collection will be of extreme value to persons desiring to consult original sources for comparative purposes. This library and archive work is of itself of the greatest importance to the Dominion.
I think I have been able in this review, with the time at my disposal, to cover pretty well the work of the department during the short time it has been in existence.

I have listened with much pleasure to the report of the acting Minister of Labour. I think that, on the whole, it is a fair and reasonable one. This, of course, is only a beginning, and there is greater scope for usefulness, although it seems that the organization is now as complete as it need be for a long time to come. But. the extent of its work could be increased very considerably. The Labour Gazette is a very valuable publication. Of course, it is not perfect ; but, it has made a very fair start, and can become very useful. There is a sufficient corps of correspondents, at the salary mentioned, to justify us in expecting the Labour Gazette to be very carefully edited. Most extreme care should be taken that nothing but reliable information shall appear in it.
When you left the Chair at six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I was speaking of the remarks of the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) in reference to my position, as he tells us he sees it in this House. I do not think it is necessary to refer further to that matter, except to say that I accept his statement when he tells us he does his best in the interest of labour. But he certainly has a handicap that does not affect me. As I understand his position, it makes no difference what the question that comes up may be, his attitude towards it is already settled. As for me. I appreciate the difficulties of that situation. I have not that to contend with myself. And I think, if the hon. gentleman will leave me out. I will endeavour to do my best as an independent. My hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Smith) was also referred to, and, as he is not able to be in his place this evening,
I think it would not be out of place for me to explain how he comes to be a member of this House. For some years he was a labour member in the British Columbia legislature, representing a constituency where the coal miner vote predominates. During the last few years the Trades Congress of this country resolved, after mature deliberation, that it would start upon a course of independent political action. At its last session in this city it asked its president, Mr. Ralph Smith, whether he would resign his seat in the British Columbia house and take his chances of election to the Dominion parliament, representing the labour interests of the country. He expressed his willingness to accede to that request. That is how he came to accept the nomination and, by a majority of votes in his district, has become its member. At a previous meeting of the Trades Congress, when he was elected as its president-and I think it is only fair to say that whatever position he has taken he has always been perfectly frank-he told- them that in British Columbia parties, as we know them in other parts of the country, were unknown. He was here as a labour representative, but in politics he had always acted with the
Liberal party ; and he told the congress : If you think it right to elect such a man as I am to he your president, I am at your service. That is how he became president of the Trades Congress, and afterwards became, at the solicitation of the members of that congress, a member of this House. For myself, I do not aspire in any way to be what is called a labour leader-or a labour follower. It is no part of my belief to have either leaders or followers. I believe that Ilia labour people should make up their minds what they want, and should insist that the men whom they elect shall carry out tlie work or stand to one side.
The acting minister has referred to the organization of the Labour Bureau. That bureau was brought into existence hy a clause of the Conciliation Bill that passed this House last year. And. after that there was passed what is called the ' current wage clause ' or ' the fair-wage clause,' and this being put into operation by the Labour Department, has become the most important Part of that department's business. The resolution passed by this House was as follows :
That it be resolved, that all government contracts should contain such conditions as will prevent abuses which may arise from the subletting of such contracts, and that every effort should be made to secure the payment of such wages as are generally accepted as current in each trade for competent workmen in the district where the work is carried out, and that this House cordially concurs in such policy and deems it the duty of the government to take immediate steps to give effect thereto. It is hereby declared that the work to which the foregoing policy should apply includes not only work undertaken by the government itself, but also all works aided by grant of Dominion public funds.
Notv, in discussing this resolution, the Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Mulock) told us that when that was passed by this House it would become operative in every department under this government. And. later on, when it was passed, I think it was on the last day of the last session, answering a question that had been put earlier in the session, he to some length went on to explain that it would apply not only to -all work done by the government, but to all work that was in any way assisted by the government, and especially would it apply to railway construction when the railways had accepted public subsidy. Now. that becomes by far the larger part of the work of the Labour Department, and I claim- and that was the point of my remarks this afternoon-that the Department of Labour should not stand at one side and merely do the clerical work, but that it is its business to see to it that the fair-wage clause is made part of every contract covered by this resolution. The Minister of Railway's and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) only last week, told us that in his department' it was not customary to include this clause, and I very

much doubt whether it is being inserted- though the acting minister can perhaps tell us-in the conditions that go with the subsidizing of railways. It should be, and it was distinctly promised us that it would be. Now, as an earnest of good faith and assurance that this resolution would be carried out, before this parliament was prorogued last year, there was a fair-wage officer appointed. And, by the way, fault has been found with that appointment, because the appointee was Mr. O'Donoghue. The hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) has complained that Mr. O'Donoghue was a politician and also a Liberal. It seems to me that either party, when it has an appointment to make, generally appoints a man of its own stripe. I think my hon. friend from East Elgin would have been much surprised if a Conservative had been appointed as fair-wage officer. But that is not the question ; the question is whether the officer who has been appointed is thoroughly competent to do the work. It is possible, of course, that many labourmen not of political stripe, would not altogether endorse his appointment. But you can not find any one who has known him for years past in the labour movement who would not say that the appointment of Mr. O'Donoghue is a first-class appointment, if you want the work properly done. That is all I claim, and all I am interested in. When a contract is to be let, before it is published, the fair-wage officer is supposed to ascertain what are the current rates of wages in the district where the work is to be carried on. He reports that to the department, and that becomes a schedule and is made a part of the contract. But it is not uncommon, in specifications for public works, that there is some deviation, and some one has to investigate and determine what is the right thing in these cases.
But I should think that where there are complaints about a violation of the fair-wage clause in a contract, the proper people to refer that to is the Department of Labour who, through this fair-wage officer, shall investigate these cases, shall determine them, and shall report to the department through whom the cheques have to go to pay the conti'actor. and that the contractor shall be told that if he has anything to pay he must pay it forthwith, and that if he refuses to do so, the department will pay the balance and deduct the amount from the contract price. I ' think that should be done altogether in the Labour Department. I mention this because we have had reason to think that this course is not being followed. It seems to me that the course that is being followed is open to grave danger, and I fear if it goes on in the way it has started that, either under this government or a succeeding government, and in some contracts, say in contracts with the friends of that government, it will be practically understood that the determination of

claims will be a very slow process ; while on the other hand and in other cases the contractor will be held strictly to the mark. Now, that matter should be properly started at the beginning ; it should be put in such form that the procedure shall go on mechanically, that the determination of these claims shall not take months but shall be done in a few days, so that the whole thing may be settled speedily ; if not,' then the value of the clause is almost completely lost, and those who are particularly interested will lose all faith in it. What is more, if the fair-wage clause is inserted in a contract, and if the contractor in tendering knows the figures, and then the department refuses to enforce them, the only result of that current wage is really to enrich the contractor more than he would have been if the current wage clause had not been there. I think that should be looked after and should be stopped.
Once again I wish to refer to the papers I asked for some weeks ago ; and I will ask the Acting Minister of Labour whether he will see that they are laid on the Table and up to date. They are in reference to the St. Andrews Locks contract, and they are important, because this is an important case. Early last year, tenders had been called for and were in before this resolution by the Postmaster General had been brought before the House, and directly it was put on the Order paper, it was resolved to send back those tenders and call for a new tender, inserting in the new tender this clause calling for a current wage, so that the contractors had a chance to figure over again, and they figured on the wage schedule that was put in. Now, directly work was done under that contract there were complaints that the schedule was not being observed. I know there are cases of honest dispute, there is lots of room for being either right or wrong. But there was a delay of nearly six months, and we cannot get the cases determined and cannot get the papers. I would ask the Acting Minister of Labour, before the vote goes through, to promise to lay those papers on the Table right up to date.

I certainly thought that the papers mentioned by the hon. gentleman had been brought down, but I must have been under a mistake. There is no objection to bringing them down, and 1 will speak to the minister and see that they are prepared as quickly as possible.

With respect to the subject mentioned by my hon. friend from Provencher (Mr. LaRiviSre) awhile ago, the distribution of this Gazette, I may say that the first occasion I ever saw a copy of the Labour Gazette was during the last election campaign, when a prominent gentleman holding a position, I believe, in one of the labour organizations in Halifax, pointed out page 15 of the Labour Gazette of September, 1900, and showed me how

this government liad passed a law, as he understood It, to compel the insertion of the fair wages clause in all contracts. Now, I venture to say that it would be better for the editor of this Gazette, whoever he may be, to endeavour to give a little more accurate account of discussions in the House of Commons, if such discussions are to be dealt with in this Labour Gazette. The discussion which took place in the House of Commons with regard to that is well known. The Postmaster General brought in a resolution, but the passage of that resolution imposed no obligation on the government, it was passed by only one branch of the legislature but not by the two branches. It was in the form of a resolution, and not in the form of a Bill. Yet the labour men throughout the country thoroughly uu-derstood from the way in which this was presented to them on page 15, that that fair-wage contract was a matter of law, a matter of legal obligation on the government, and I found a good deal of difficulty in convincing people with whom I talked on the subject in Halifax that such was not the case, simply because it was not accurately stated on this page. The facts of the case are well known. In the discussiou which took place in the House of Commons, Sir Charles Tupper, the then leader of the opposition, Mr. Nicholas Flood Davin and others urged that the government should bring this in, not as a resolution, but in the form of a Bill, which would be obligatory upon the government and would compel obedience to it. I am not disposed to find undue fault with the way in which this has been dealt with in the Labour Gazette, and what I say is more by way of caution for the future ; because, if this Labour Gazette and this Labour Department are to be of any use in this country, it is perfectly apparent to every person that they must be kept free from any tinge of partisanship. I would venture to suggest to the Acting Postmaster General that if he is employing as correspondents of this paper active political partisans, he is not doing his duty with regard to such matters ; because the reports of gentlemen taking an active part in politics are more or less liable to be influenced by their political opinions. The gentleman who edits this Gazette will not know to what extent these reports are influenced by those political opinions, and I think that so far as it may be necessary to select correspondents, it is extremely desirable that persons should be selected whose opinions are not likely to be unduly biassed by any political views they may happen to entertain.

I can hardly agree with the hon. gentleman that anything on page 15 of the September issue would mislead any person into supposing that the resolution referred to was a law, or anything else than what it really was.

Permit me to point it out. I venture to say that the gentleman with whom I discussed this matter in Halifax, so far as natural ability is concerned, is the peer of almost any man in this House, and I venture to say that had he had the opportunities of education that others in this House have enjoyed, he might have taken a very prominent position in this country, because he is one of the most able and intelligent men with whom I ever conversed, and he was thoroughly convinced from reading this that such was the case. At the bottom of column one on this page, it is stated in so many words :
The passing of the resolution placed an obligation upon the government, not only in respect to the advertised contracts, but bound it in regard to all future contracts.
Well, does my hon. friend pretend to tell me that any labouring man in this country, or any other intelligent man, reading that, would not understand it exactly in the way in which this gentleman did understand it ? I think my hon. friend could not have observed these words, or he would not have made the statement that he did make. I venture to think that there are few labouring men in this country who could bring a more acute mind, so far as natural abilities are concerned, to bear upon the consideration of these words than the man with whom I conversed, and it was only with the utmost possible difficulty, after a long argument and after getting a copy of ' Hansard ' and showing him the debate in the House of Commons, that I was able to satisfy him as to what was the position which the parties had taken, and what was the result of the resolution which the House had passed.

It may be possible that the gentleman who read this might be under a misapprehension. At the same time, I think my hon. friend will admit that so far as this article is concerned, it is a mere statement of fact, and that if there is anything in it that would be misleading, it is not intentional.
I said to my hon. friend that I was not desirous of finding undue fault. What I said was more by way of caution for the future than by way of criticism.

I was coming to that. As to the opinion, that the passing of the clause would impose an obligation upon the government and upon parliament, I think the gentleman who read it would be quite right in coming to that conclusion. When that resolution was passed, I think that the government and parliament should regard it as an obligation to be carried out.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. A moral obligation.

Yes, a moral obligation which, to my mind, is more important very often than a good many legal obligations. I agree with the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Borden), that the slightest digression in the publishing of the Labour Gazette to give it a political complexion, or that it should be used for party purposes, would be a most regrettable thing. If the department is to be of any use in the publication of the Labour Gazette, it can only be so by maintaining that publication as a purely independent paper, and giving statistical information and facts, and not opinions. I may say to my hon. friend, that the instructions of the department to the correspondents are, that they are not to give opinions and that opinions will not be accepted. Their correspondence must be altogether limited to a statement of facts. I think they have carried out that instruction to the fullest extent. The editor might, iu publishing an article, not be familiar with the local conditions, and pass something that would have a loeal effect politically, no matter how conscientious and desirous he might be in regard to anything of that kind. If the instructions are carried out that opinions are not to be given, but that correspondents must confine themselves to statements of fact, there would be no room for complaint. These statements are open to correction if they are not correct. Certainly no correspondent would be kept in connection with the department who would be found to be unreliable. So far as the department is concerned, I think these instructions will be enforced to the letter, because, I agree with the hon. gentleman, that the only way to make the Gazette useful to the country, to the employers and the employed, is by making it a paper thoroughly reliable, giving only facts and statistics in accordance with the plan originally laid down.

I hope the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Borden) is not trying to excuse the hon. My hon. friend (Mr. Puttee) knows. I suppose, why it was done in that way in the British House of Commons ? If he does not, perhaps it would be worth his while to inquire.

I wish to refer to one statement made by my hon. friend from East Sirncoe (Mr. Bennett), as he connected my name with it; that is. the statement with reference to the character of the enforcement of the provisions of the Alien Labour law by the government. The only

3S18
criticism with regard to that matter which 1 have heard from parties who are conversant with the facts, has been that the government have erred on the side of severity ; and the fact that under the operations of the Labour Department 56 men have been deported from Canada within the last, few, months is in my opinion a proof that the provisions of the Act have been stringently enforced. Since the debate took place in this House on this question some days ago, I have ascertained that the deportation of aliens from Canada has been many fold greater than the deportation of Canadian aliens from the United States, and that the law is more stringently enforced in this country than it is in the United States. I have the statement of Mr. DeBarry, the immigration agent of the United States at Buffalo, that the operations of the Canadian law are of a wholesale character, while the operations of the United States law are of a retail character in comparison. With regard to the cases on the north shore of the Georgian Bay referred to by my hon. friend, the complaints received were investigated on the ground by Mr. Williams, of the Labour Bureau ; and Mr. Williams certainly exercised discretion and at the same time firmness in the discharge of his duties. A considerable number of men were sent from the employment of the Michigan Land Company and the Eddy Lumber Company, who were engaged in the erection of sawmills. These deportations were considered by these firms to be cases of hardship, and I believe in reality they were such ; but it was impossible for Mr. Williams to act otherwise than he did in the matter. The position occupied by these firms is substantially this. They were erecting extensive saw-mills at a cost of several hundred thousand dollars, in a sparsely settled country where labour could not be obtained. One of these firms sent an agent to Ottawa to employ men, and he remained here a couple of weeks and succeeded in securing five. These firms, who are transferring theiir manufacturing operations from the United States to Canada, and who have been engaged in business for years, have of course in their employ as skilled labourers, filers of band saws, sawyers, &c., men whose capacities and qualifications they know thoroughly well. A mistake made in the employment of one of these skilled labourers might involve the loss of thousands of dollars ; it might imperil the operations of the whole concern ; and these men asked to be allowed to bring to this country, for the purpose of settling them 'here, a class of skilled labourers whom they employed in the United States, and who were capable of discharging the duties they required of them properly and efficiently. I hold that the deportation of men of that kind is a mistake. We are asking for immigration ; we are paying agents to traverse Europe for the purpose of securing
immigration ; and in my belief it is not in our interest to repel a class of immigrants coming from the United States who are of superior intelligence to the class which we try to secure at a considerable cost from Europe. This cry about the enforcement of the Alien Labour law is something which I have no sympathy with whatever ; and 1 affirm, from knowledge of the fact, that the enforcement of the law in the United States is more liberal and less stringent than the enforcement of the law here. If the American authorities were to put into force the regulations which my hon. friend from East Simcoe asks that we should enforce, to-morrow morning 500 men would! be prevented from crossing from Windsor to Detroit to engage in their daily avocations ; 100 would be stopped at Sarnia, and 100 at Fort Erie, and thousands of Canadians on the border would be prevented from passing forward and back to the employment which they obtain across the border to their own financial advantage. For these reasons I have no sympathy with the position taken by my hon. friend from East Simcoe and by other hon. gentlemen on the opposite side of the House with reference to this matter. So far as the enforcement of this law is concerned, X hold that no well-founded criticism can be applied to the operations of the Labour Bureau in Canada. The law has been enforced with a sufficient degree of efficiency-with a greater degree, in my belief, than is in the public interest. I have very little more to say with reference to this matter except that I do not believe it is in the interests of Canada to impede the expenditure of money in this country and to throw obstacles in the way of men who wish to invest large sums in industrial enteiprises. I am sorry to see a disposition manifested to embarrass the government in this mtftter, and I fear this disposition can only proceed from a desire to throw discredit upon the government by appealing to prejudices with regard to alien labour.
The hon. gentleman from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) indulged in some facetious remarks with reference to some item about bartenders and so forth. I suppose that the Labour Gazette, or any other publication which deals with the interests of labour, if closely scrutinized, will be found to contain some little items which, considered apart from the rest, may look a little ridiculous, but we must remember that this Gazette was only inaugurated a short time ago and must necessarily contain some imperfections at the outset, which no doubt will be gradually removed. But, I think that the intention is a good one and the operations of this publication will grow more and more beneficial in the public interest from month to month as it proceeds.	*

Mr. LaRIVIERE. Whose fault is it that we have not seen it before ?

Since the first number was issued, I have been a constant reader of it, and our hon. friends had the same opportunity of writing to have a copy sent them. I have read it with a great deal of interest because I believe that the news it contains is absolutely true. One of the great difficulties I have experienced in connection with labour journals, is that the news they give is not always accurate, but generally biassed, and sometimes they have other interests to subserve besides those of labour. The only way in which this journal can be made useful is to make it absolutely nonpolitical ; and from the first number I have read to the last, X have never seen an article or reference of a political nature, or in any way calculated to advance the interests of a particular party. Just as soon as this journal is used to aid in the advancement of either political party, its usefulness will disappear, and I do trust that our hon. friends opposite, before they condemn or even asperse it, will peruse one number after another and judge the publication on its general merits. There is no fairness in taking any one report, such as that from Vancouver, as a specimen of the whole, and even that particular item may be interesting to a great number of men who earn their livelihood in the way indicated. But the articles I have read struck me as being the very reverse of what they have been described here to-night, when it was said that each correspondent is a political heeler. I look forward with considerable confidence to this journal being of great use to the people. Now, I am not going to enter into a dispute with the hon. gentleman as to whether these men are political hacks, or as to whether the information contained in the Gazette is of the character he described ; but, I will leave it to the large number of people who have an opportunity of studying this Gazette to judge as to whether it is, as I have represented, a most useful publication. i will trouble the committee with reading another letter with regard to the work of the department, because when the hon. gentleman said that the work the country desired this department to perform was with regard to alien labour, he forgot to realize the importance of the work that was being done under the Conciliation Act, as well as other matters to which I referred some time ago. I will read this letter from a firm well known In this country :
Dundas, Ont., Jan. 29, 1901. Hon. ffm, . Mulock, M.P.
Department of Labour, Ottawa, Ont.
Sir,-We have the honour to acknowledge receipt of your courteous favour of the 26th Inst., and in reply we desire to express our pleasure in meeting your deputy, Mr. King, and also to say that there is no doubt but that owing to his good judgment the slight difficulty which

(Sgd.) JOHN BERTRAM & SONS.
I think John Bertram & Sons are well known to be not supporters of the Liberal party, but active and prominent politicians, and I think this expression of their views with regard to the good work done on that particular occasion will be accepted as an honest expression. Certainly, I think we may safely appeal to the committee and say, that In the good work done already we have saved far more to the country in actual money, in settlements under the Conciliation Act, than the whole expenditure of the department. I agree with the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) that every effort must be made by the minister and the officials of the department to keep party politics out of it, and that we are in a position to succeed to a very great extent in connection with the Labour Gazette, I think, shows, that that is the intention of the government that their instructions have been followed to the letter, and I trust it will be continued in such a way as to give satisfaction to all concerned.
I would like to ask the hon. member by what authority all these expenditures have been made. " Did parliament vote any money last year ?
You are referring to the expenditure for the current year ?
For the current year.

We are on the estimate for the coming year. But, as to that question, I will give the information when the estimates comes up for the current year if that would satisfy the hon. gentleman. There was an estimate made, but I am not familiar with the figures now.

We have no record of It here. It appears to me that the utmost care should be taken and has not been taken to prevent this from becoming largely a political machine. Look over the Gazette. He might have added that eighteen days after the meeting the parliament of Canada was dissolved, that the right hon. leader of the government (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and the hon. Postmaster General Mr. WALLACE.
(Hon. Mr. Mulock) were then making their preparations to rope in the electorate and that this condescending attendance at the meeting of the Trades and Labour Congress was to assist them in their Dominion elections which were right on, which they knew were on, but which the people of Canada were not informed about. Everything points to the fact that everything was utilized by the hon. ministers to advance their political fortunes. The city of Toronto

Mr. McCarthy. They defeated the labour candidates in Toronto.

Not only the city of Toronto, but the whole province of On-

tario, by an overwhelming majority, declared against the hon. gentleman and we are all workingmen in Ontario. The whole of the reports in this Labour Gazette, after a cursory examination, appear to me to indicate that it is pretty much of a campaign document. This is the October number, issued immediately before the election, and it is devoted to advancing the interests of the Liberal party. You cannot find a line in it that has anything to say for the members of the loyal opposition, but you can find plenty in it eulogizing the government of Canada. Another thing that we may fairly make objection to, and which has been referred to is the fact that we have, here, among all the members of parliament who have only seen this publication to-night, one copy for each of the eight months during which it has been issued. I am informed that every member of this House was sent a circular asking him to send in the names of persons to whom he would wish a copy of the Gazette sent, just as was the member for Toronto (Mr. Clarke) who answered the letter. I have no recollection of having received that circular. I repudiate the hon. gentleman's assertion that he is in the same position as I am in this matter. He is responsible, for it is he who should have had copies sent to members of parliament. This is the only publication of parliament that has not been sent to the representatives of the people, and so we are asked to vote $50,000 without having had an opportunity of considering the work that has been done. I may say that the appointment of men like D. ,T. O'Donoghue will not give satisfaction to the people of Toronto. Hei has been a political partisan of most pronounced type. He cannot get out of the rut; he is too old now, X suppose. There are plenty of men of their own poll tical stripe whose selection by the government would have given confidence to the people that fairness would have been exercised, but I do not think that can be said
of Mr. O'Donoghue by those who know him best where he has lived longest. The salaries that are paid and all the expenses con nected with it have been on an extravagant scale for the initiation of a new departure. The minister shakes his head, and thinks, I suppose, that it is a most modest equipment and that the salaries are low. I do not think so. I believe there could have been and should have been more efficient work done for much less expenditure.

If we devote our attention to the discussion of this question with a view of really helping the organization of the Labour Department, this is an important question and good will result. No. It is like a newspaper report that ia given.

This is the very best guar antee of the character of Mr. O'Donoghue.

I make that statement on reliable information and if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wallace) declares it is not correct I will withdraw it.
I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fraser) is correct.
Is the hon. member for West York satisfied now ?
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fraser) did not know.

It was my fear that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wallace) would not accept my statement which made me quake until the member for Elgin (Mr. Ingram) came to my assistance. Now, in view of the fact that the labour organizations Who are most interested in this bureau, and who know more about Mr. COMMONS
O'Donoghue tlian anybody else, have resolved that this gentleman should be appointed, I ask the hon, gentleman (Mr. Wallace) if it is fair to the labour organizations and to Mr. O'Donoghue for him to state in this House that Mr. O'Donoghue is not satisfactory to the labouring men of the city of Toronto. It just sho-ws how ready some people are to asperse a man's character when they have nothing but party ends in view. Labour is neither Liberal nor Tory. There are men in the labour organizations who belong to both parties, but perhaps if the workingmen knew the history of the labour question in this country there would be fewer of them in the ranks of the Tory party. In 1886 the late government appointed a Royal Commission to inquire into the relations of labour and capital and all subjects connected therewith, and when do you think that commission made its report ? Why, not until three years afterwards. So anxious were they to ascertain all the facts, so anxious were they that labour and capital should be brought together, and so anxious were they that the report should be characterized by wisdom that it took three long years to prepare it, and I am bound to say that that report contains information which would lead thoughtful men to think that there was a labour question in this country which should be attended to.
Are you quite sure the report was not made until three years after 1886 ?

The commission was appointed in 1S86 and the report was given in on the 22nd of February, 18S9, between two and three years afterwards. This is what that labour commission said :
Your committee are firmly persuaded that the interests of the working people will be promoted if all matters relating to them be placed under the administration of one of the ministers of the Crown, so that a labour bureau be established, statistics collected, information disseminated-
Just the very thing that is being done.
-and the working people find readier means of making known their needs and desires to the government.
And on page 121 are set forth detailed reasons why this Bureau of Labour Statistics should be created. It is there again stated :
The testimony of all the witnesses was to the effect that a bureau of labour statistics for the Dominion is generally needed.
It is further stated :
to provide for the Collection and Publishing of Labour Statistics. I have that Act now before me. It provides for a branch of the Department of Agriculture known as the Bureau of Labour Statistics, and hon. gentlemen will find it as chapter 15 of 53 Victoria. It provides :
The Governor in Council may from time to time appoint an officer who shall be called the Assistant Commissioner of Labour Statistics, and who shall hold office during pleasure.
The duties of the commissioner shall be to collect, classify and arrange and present in quarterly bulletins and yearly reports to parliament statistics relating to all kinds of labour in Canada.
It shall be the duty of the commissioner to collect from Dominion, provincial and municipal officers, and from all officers of any public institutions

And so on-all this information. The head of this Bureau of Labour Statistics was to be the Minister of Agriculture, who was to be called the Commissioner of Labour Statistics. The sum of $10,000, the same sum as before, was appropriated from the consolidated fund for the purpose of running that bureau. There is a schedule annexed to the Act, for the classification of statistics, showing exactly .what should be done. Now, here comes a curious little episode. I remember running an election in 1891-and in the jjrovince of Nova Scotia we have a large numbei of workingmen, both in our mines and in industrial pursuits. In fact, what makes Nova Scotia the greatest province of the Dominion is that we all have to work there, and those who work know best how to enjoy life and make the most of it. In Nova Scotia we passed legislation of this kind two or three years before the Dominion. That legislation we found very effective. But what I want to draw particular attention to is that in the election of 1891, from one end of the province to the other, the cry was : Look at what the government are doing for labour ; they have formed a bureau ; they have voted money for it ; they are going to gather statistics ; this is the first government that ever thought of labour, and you will vote for it. And I am bound to say that in 1S91 they did get a large proportion of the labour vote in the province of Nova Scotia. But what happened ? Although that Act was passed in 1890, not one step was taken during the whole time the party opposite were in power, and they went out of power in 1896 without ever having done anything to have labour statistics collected. But the Labour Bureau is now in operation.
Where all the witnesses who were indicated on this point gave identically the same reply, it would he useless to point out any particular testimony as showing the need of a Dominion bureau.
That was the report of this commission in February, 1889. The report was laid before parliament in the session of 1890, and the government of that day passed an Act
We are in the twentieth century now.

Yes, and you will have much to forget in the past, so far as the action of your political friends in regard to labour is concerned. The Act constituting this Labour Bureau was passed last year, and it went immediately into opera-

tion ; that is just the difference. It can not be expected that everything is going to be perfected in the first few months of its 'operation ; but I am bound to state that the Gazette is a very respectable journal for the purposes for which it was created. One benefit that will be derived from this Bureau of Labour and the statistics that are being collected, will be of immense advantage to the Dominion of Canada. If 1 read the signs of the times aright, I think our neighbours to the south of us are fast coming to a clash ; and one of the things which we in Canada should learn above all others, is that labour and capital ought to understand each other, that the interests of both are reciprocal, that capital ought to help labour as labour ought to help capital ; and much can be done by inculcating beforehand the proper principles relating to labour and capital by which those who work and those who invest money will understand each other. That is one of the difficulties occurring in the nation to the south just now. So chronic is the state of things in the United States that at any time the very smallest amount of powder may cause a great explosion. Labour there feels that it is down-trodden, that it has not its proper position, and the capital that is invested is being gathered into large combinations. The fight is going to be between labour on the one hand and that of accumulation of capital on the other. Now, if you have in Canada an educative process going on year after year, by which those who invest money and those who labour can be brought together to discuss matters, you will have a better understanding ; and when you have labour feeling that it is fairly used, and that it is receiving not only at the hands of the capital which employs it, but at the hands of the government, such consideration ns it ought to have, you will have a condition of things that will make peaceful industry in this country. That was one of the reasons why I rejoiced last year at the establishment of this bureau. I am not concerned whether a man was a strong politician before he took office or not. There are strong politicians who are still, I am bound to say, honest men. I do not see that the fact that a man was a strong Tory or a strong Liberal before he took office, should disqualify him from making truthful reports of the condition of things in the district in which he lives. Must it be laid down as a rule that a man who is a jelly fish, who has had no political views at all, Is the only man to be employed to send reports ?

Let me explain that the objection made to Mr. O'Donoghue is not the objection which the hon. gentleman is stating. He is putting up a straw man and knocking it down. The objection was this, that Mr. O'Donoghue had been a government official for many years, and that during the whole time he has been also a political partisan, and of course he will continue to be.
I shall have to ask my hon. friend to settle that question with the hon. member for East Simcoe, who called him a political hack.
That is what we say, although he has been in the employ of the Ontario government for the last dozen years or so.

And a political partisan during the whole of that time.
Supposing he was, he is a political hack, because he was employed by a local government.
No, because he was a political partisan and working in the interests of a political party while he was taking the money of the whole people of Canada.

I would remind the hon. gentleman that he is just as likely to be as wrong in that statement as he was in the statement that Mr. O'Donoghue was not recommended by the workingmen of Canada. He said that the workingmen were all in favour of the present opposition, and yet, these are the men who recommended this political hack to be employed in this work.
Oh, no.
Was not Mr. O'Donoghue recommended by the labouring men in the city of Toronto ?
No.

He -was not recommended by the Labour Congress of the Dominion, but in the president's address to the members of the Labour Congress of Canada, he approved of Mr. O'Donoghue's nomination, but it was not the workingmen of Canada who approved of it.
I am informed that he was approved by the labour organizations of the city of Toronto.
Give us the information.
If the hon. gentleman is going to put -me under a catechetical examination, I must decline to be catechised.
If the hon. gentleman will say that he knows it of his own personal knowledge, I shall not dispute his statement.

I am informed, on as good authority as the hon. gentleman, and it will be for the hon. gentleman to disprove my statement. Is it objected that Mr. O'Donoghue is not a good official and that his j work is not good work ?

That is the charge made.
I make that statement.

If the hon. gentleman says so, that is some evidence, bult it is not conclusive, because if it were reported to him that Mr. O'Donoghue had ever in any way opposed him In politics, he would, no doubt, feel that this man was his enemy. I can quite understand his feeling in that regard.
The hon. gentleman is entirely too innocent.

The question of my innocence being admitted, I can proceed to discuss this matter apart from personal considerations. The governemnt is to be commended on its policy in publishing this labour journal. From time to time that Labour Gazette has been productive of much good. The workingmen with whom I have come in contact have expressed themselves as vastly pleased with it. But, I have one objection to raise, and that is, that it has only one agent in Nova Scotia, and he is in the city of Halifax. I would inform the hon. minister that in Sydney and Pictou there .are more men employed in mines and manufactures than in Halifax, and there is no agent in either of these places. No doubt the gentleman employed at Halifax is an excellent man, who sends from time to time to the Gazette a good deal of information about these other places. Hon. gentlemen opposite have admitted that this is a step in the right direction, and no doubt improvements will be made, and it seems to me that this House, as a whole, should give this scheme its generous support. Talk of its costing $50,000. Why, one strike would cost the people a great deal more. A strike of a week in any large establishment will cost, both in time lost to the labourers employed and the loss to the establishment itself, far more than we are expending on this publication, labour has a place in this country which we must recognize more and more. The fact that we have been doing all we could to promote the investment of capital and thus advance the interests of capital, is one of the best reasons why we should give labour every advantage we can. and there is no better way of doing this than by disseminating all necessary information which will be of value to the workingmen, and thus help in securing to them the position they ought to hold in the country. We should take every means to give them an education that will enable them to make their influence felt, not only in political circles, but in the wider social sphere, and thus promote their interests in every respect.

I am not sure whether it would be advisable to carry this discussion any further, but as I have been a labourer since I was twelve years Mr. FRASER.
old, and have always been a producer of wealth, I think I ought to say a word on this labour question. This government is the first in Canada which has had the courage to inaugurate a department for the purpose of looking after the interests of our workingmen. It seems that previous governments were asked to do the same thing before, but failed to respond to the demand, and it remained for this government to embark on this new undertaking. But, until I arrived at Ottawa. I laboured under the misfortune of being ignorant that there was any such publication as the Labour Gazette, and I do not know that I would have discovered its existence had I not been present at one of the committees, where I learned all about it, and I was pleased to learn that something was being done in the interests of labour by this government. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Fraser) comes from the province of Nova Scotia, which has produced many things that merit our commendation, and in this case it has produced certainly a great man, because I believe he is the largest man in the House. That hon. gentleman has told us that labour and capital are growing further apart every day. Anything that will bring about a reconciliation and settle matters in dispute between labour and capital will do a grand work for this country. I think I remember reading some years ago that the Prime Minister on one occasion took upon himself to interfere, and went to a gang of railway labourers and settled some question of dispute between them and their employer. If I am mistaken, I am willing to be corrected ; but if the right hon. gentleman did that, he accomplished a great thing. This Labour Gazette which is published monthly and sent out to a large number of people-it has not been sent to you Tory members as yet, but you will get it as you have criticised it so severely-I believe is calculated to do a great deal of good. At any rate, it will show the labouring man where labour is in demand. They will see, for instance, that in St. Thomas there is a large armoury going up and $50,000 being expended, and so we may look for an influx of labouring men. But, best of all, the gentleman who presides over this department will have an oppor tunity of settling labour disputes. I understand that he was successful in settling the Valleyfield dispute. If that gentleman or any other can settle these labour difficulties, he will do a great deal of good, for when a strike takes place the men who have been at work must seek labour across the line or elsewhere, and the town where they lived sees them no more.
Now, I wish to say one word with regard to the Alien Labour question. I believe that the Prime Minister has a Bill before the House, which may have passed before now. But when I heard hon. gentlemen discussing that question a few evenings ago, I

felt as if X would like to speak upon it. We learned the other day that we are spending half a million of money every year in bringing immigrants into this country. We have been going to all parts of Europe to look for them. We have been told that our agents have found in Southern Europe a people without a name, and some of these they are going to bring to Canada. And yet this Alien Labour law is to keep out of the country many good citizens such as we are bringing from Europe, the most intelligent and advanced men, mechanics and skilled labourers, whom we ought to encourage to come to this country. The greatest country the world has ever seen has risen to the height she has because she has made her home an asylum for the distressed and oppressed of all the nations of the world. And we would do well to take an example from her, and let every man of industry come here. That is what we want in this country, and not to bar people out by an Alien I.abour law. I feel that I would like to launch out on this subject. Why, we can hardly get men or women to assist us on our farms ; we are obliged to do the labour ourselves because we cannot find men to hire. And yet you want to pass a law to keep men from coming to us from the country to the south of us. I am told that this is a retaliatory law. We all know what retaliation means. Hon. members when they were young, no doubt, rend Bacon's Essays-if not, they ought to have done so. Bacon says that the man who seeks revenge is only keeping his own wounds green. And that is what we are doing by retaliating upon our neighbours. Let us set them a good example ; let us invite them to come here. I am satisfied that our workingmen have brains enough and ability enough to compete with all comers. Let us keep people here when they come ; but to do that we must keep them cheaply. Men must be able to live here more cheaply than in any other place in the world, and then you will get them to come. Before sitting down, I have only to repeat that I hope the Labour Department will be kept up. But you must not have political hacks sending information to this Labour Gazette. I do not say that that is the case now, but If it is the case a change should be made. There are men in every section, men upon whom you can rely, men who are not political hacks, who will send you that information gratis. The Bureau of Industries was started in Ontario some years ago. I have been one of the correspondents of that bureau since its inception, and I never got a red cent for anything that I ever did.
Put in your bill.

No, I shall not put in a bill. There need be no trouble about getting this information. In every town and city there are labour organizations-and I want to tell hon. members that
some of the ablest and the most intelligent men belong to these labour bodies in the towns and cities. I can tell hon. gentlemeu that when it comes to discussing political questions, they are not in it with some of the members of these labour organizations. These gentlemen would be quite willing to send you the information without charge, if you will furnish them with paper and postage. I do not think it is necessary to pay $100 a year to some fellow beeausq he is one of your party men. Select the best man in a locality and ask him if he will be kind enough to report the condition of labour there, and you can get the information. My advice to hon. gentlemen opposite is to keep on publishing this Labour Gazette, but in their own interests let them make it unpartisan, because the men on this side will be in power some day, and the government will have reason to be sorry if they set them a bad example.

I am glad to hear the remarks of my hon. colleague from West Elgin (Mr. Robinson). Knowing his past history, I know that he has always taken an active interest in labour questions. Reference has been made to the fact that only a limited supply of the Labour Gazette has been sent out. My experience has been this.
