I am inclined to think that the Deputy Minister of Labour, so far as he is personally concerned, is eager to publish this Gazette from a non-partisan standpoint. But I fully recognize the great difficulties that he is under in publishing this Gazette as a non-partisan publication, surrounded as he is with persons who have always been most active partisans. I desire to warn the deputy minister to be very careful as to the advice that he receives from those men who are associated with him in that department. For one, I may mention Mr. D. J. O'Donoghue, who has been one of the most active partisans for a number of years in the Dominion of Canada.
Will the hon. gentleman tell us the position that Mr. O'Donoghue occupied at the time that he was appointed to the position he now holds ?
What right had he to assume that the Senate would not pass it ?
Will the hon. member please answer that question I asked him a lflomeut ago, and tell us the position Mr. O'Donoghue held in the labour council at the time he was appointed ?

If the hon. gentleman will possess his soul in patience I will tell him before I take my seat. Is it not a fact-and if I am incorrect in the statement I make, let that statement be corrected to-morrow and I will withdraw it-it is a fact that these very labour men were told to go to Mr. Jackson, and did go to Mr. Jackson, who knew all about that question, and he would explain to them the exact position they were in, and the reasons why this government could not grant the legislation that they were asking for ? There is a certain gentleman occupying a position in another place within this building, who offered to take them to the law clerk of that institution in another part of this building, and that law clerk would explain to them the exact position the government was in with respect to giving legislation such as they asked for ? Did they go and take the opportunity of finding this out ? No, that did not suit their purpose. What did they want ? They wanted to go to that other place in this building, believing as they did, after canvassing to some extent, that the legislation they were asking for would be thrown out, and then they would have another opportunity of having a slap at that institution, for political purposes only. This is another reason why, 1 say, these gentlemen are not advocating what they believe to be in the interest of labour, but are advocating what they believe to be in the interest of a political party. Now I wish to refer to another gentleman, Mr. A. F. Jury. I was a member of the Trade and Labour Congress of Canada at the time when Alf. Jury thought it was' his duty to come to my constituency and stump the constituency against me. It was an act of brotherly love-men in the labour congress together-it was simply an act of brotherly love. I have the testimony of those who know that a very great deal of good has been accomplished. That, of course, is an expenditure from which I can show no revenue. Then as regards the railway reports, in and out, I can show no revenue either, because, as in the case of Depot Harbour, men have to be placed to attend to the transhipping of grain passing in bond from which we derive no revenue, but we have to pay these officers their salaries. New railways are coming across the border and continually demands are being made upon me to give facilities to the transportation service, from which we derive no direct benefit at all. I have ventured to make this statement because when gentlemen opposite simply put their fingers on the increased expenditure without considering it in the light of the increased business done, they might perhaps think that as great prudence as should be exercised had not been exercised in the department. I put it to any fair-minded man in the House, in view of the enormously increased business and the comparatively small increase of expenditure: I put it to him if he does not believe that there has been an efficient and economic working of the department on the part of the different officers who are concerned.
How is that $44,000 increase divided up ?

It is almost wholly in connection with the statistical branch. When we organized the
statistical branch we had to work under a disadvantage. Last year we had to get out the usual trade and navigation returns under which our usual staff that compiled these returns had to continue that work at the various ports. They had to compile under the old system the last quarter's work at the various ports, before they could come to Ottawa to engage in the work here. Last year I got a special vote of $15,000 to pay some extra men to do the work of opening the books here, preparatory to the men finishing their last year's work at their ports, which required two or three weeks. I do not ask the $15,000 this year because it is included in the $44,000, but the statistical branch will cost in the neighbourhood of $44,000. As I have said, I am asking the House to trust me with a little latitude in that respect, because when the officers become thoroughly efficient I may perhaps be able to get along with fewer hands, though I have not much hope in that respect.
I could give the names of the officers to the hon. gentleman, for I .recognize that the committee has a perfect right to have the details. We have in that statistical dedepartment altogether between sixty and sixty-five officers, including the ten or eleven whom we had before in the inside service, who got out those statistical returns. I am glad to say that my predecessor, who is taking the part of a friendly critic tonight, approves of the bringing of this statistical work to Ottawa. I find that it was talked of before I took office, but my predecessors seemed to be afraid to ask parliament for the amount it would involve, and they never carried it out. But it seemed to me to be of such importance that I thought I could safely ask parliament to grant $40,000 or $50,000 more to attain that object. Hon. gentlemen know the position in which the trade and navigation returns have been for years. My hon. friend found fault because I had not got the returns down 'this year earlier than I did. We were working under the disadvantage of inaugurating a new system, yet I find, on comparison, that the returns were on the Table this year as early or earlier than in previous years. We know how formerly the returns which were brought down to the end of June of a certain year were not laid on the Table by myself or by my predecessors until January or February of the following year, so that they were stale and unprofitable for the business community or anybody else. The result was that if I was asked in this House for a return up to a certain date, I would have to ask for time to write to the different ports to get the information. What we are working for now is that at the end of the second month there shall be a | ful report of the previous month's trade ' and commerce of the whole Dominion, in as full detail as is found in the trade and navigation return. The business men of

this country value it, the members of this House value it, and I am sure there will be no difficulty in the House granting me this vote for that purpose. If I could serve any good purpose, I could give the names of the officers and their salaries, and I will give them cheerfully if the hon. gentleman desires them.

I do not require the names. The hon. minister has taken up a very long time in establishing a comparison between what occurred in 1894-5 and the state of the department to-day. I was curious to find out exactly and with some detail how the item of $44,000 was divided up. But I will take the hon. gentleman's word for it.
I do not think we have ever listened to a more unfair or dishonest statement than the minister has made to the House to-night.
Order.
That is parliamentary, and it is true.
I understood the hon. gentleman to say dishonest. That is not parliamentary.
Quite parliamentary, and I will endeavour to prove it.
Use a kinder word.

I will make it kinder ; I do not wish to say anything harsh. We asked for information about the expenditure of $44,000 additional for this special service, and the minister gets up and beclouds all his statements, and gives not a particle of information as to why he should have spent the additional thousands he spent last year, and why he should spend the additional thousands he proposes to spend during the coming year. The same work is to be done. He has transferred his staff to Ottawa to do it here ; but he has not increased their salaries. On the contrary, he has told us that he has put them outside the pale of the inside service, because they might demand the $50 statutory increase which we on this side of the House say should be given, but he says should not be given except in some special cases. The work is the same as before, and yet he is taking $44,000 more to do it. He says that we on this side of the House were in favour of it, that we were proposing to do it, but that we were afraid to ask parliament for the increased expenditure necessary. It never came up as a very important matter for consideration ; but I do not see why there should be any increase, seeing that the officers do not receive any more pay. He tells us that he wants the money voted in a lump sum, because he may want to appoint an assistant at Midland, and he wants to have sufficient funds

so that he can take that out of the appropriation for the province on Ontario. The Minister of Customs should have some knowledge of his department. He claims that he is the only one, apparently, who has any knowledge of it; but he has to go to the hon. member for East Simcoe to get the information that an additional man to perform the work of bonding is required at the port of Midland. Did he not know that himself ? Were not his inspectors, increased as they are now, able to report as to the needs of the different ports of the Dominion ? He seems to lament that he is the only one who has ever understood the work of the Customs Department. We all know that a large portion of the customs service consists in the appointment of preventive officers, that another large portion is the appointing of officers to perform such duties as the bonding of goods through the country, which are not productive of revenue ; and then he tells a harrowing tale about the smuggling down on the lower St. Lawrence, and how he stopped it. It was all stopped before he was in the department.
No, no.

Yes. We had an effective service. We engaged Captain May with his steamer, and I received the thanks of many of the priests, who were most ardent helpers of the Customs Department, for having stamped out the smuggling that was going on and the ruining of their parishoners. So that the minister, when he gets up and says that he has been doing all these things, implying that nothing was done before he came in, is making misleading statements and statements which are not accurate, to use a mild term. He says we have increased expenditure, but look at the increase in business. In 1895 there were $17,000,000 collected, and in 1897 $28,000,000. an increase of 01 per cent in the collections and only 10 per cent in the expenses. But why did he not quote the figures he is asking us to vote to-night and say there was $212,000 increase between those two years instead of $157,000. And the year of all years which he chose to make a comparison with is one in which there was the greatest depression. But the staff was there, and we could not dismiss any of the permanent staff, because while there was a great depression, and while we were reducing the expenditure year by year, the fact that the depression would be only temporary, and when there would be an increase in business the staff would be more fully employed. In times of depression the staff are not worked to their full capacity, but that is no reason for making reductions in the staff. Since these gentlemen have come in they are expending $220,000 more than we did. Take the statistical branch, they are only furnishing us with the same information with which we have been furnished all along, and yet the

business is not as promptly done, because we were weeks in parliament before we could get the Trade and Navigation Returns, which should have been in our hands before parliament met at all. The trade returns are made up to the 1st July, 1900, and we only got the report eight months after that date.

The increase in the collection of revenue must be always followed by an increase of labour. If you have 20.000 to 30,000 entries more, look at the calculations that have to be made. There is no item in those entries but has to be carefully gone over before it can be entered in the statistics. If there is an increase in the importations, a larger quantity of goods must go to the appraisers' department to be examined. There must be men to watch the im-. ports landed, and while the St. Lawrence may be protected to some extent, that only turns the attention of smugglers to the coast of Cape Breton. And the liquor that used to be smuggled up the St. Lawrence they succeeded, in some instances, in landing in Cape Breton. So that that work has been prevented by the steamer that has been engaged in that service out of the port of Sydney. I am sure that the hon. gentleman must know that the increase of revenue must mean an increase in labour, and that the statistical branch must increase in proportion to the others. My complaint with regard to the Minister of Customs is that he does not apply for sufficient money for the services of his department. I wanted, in one or two instances, to have ports of entry opened in my own constituency, and the reply that I got was that the minister had no money. That is a very convenient reply, but I do not see the reason why he should not have money when this government and this House is willing to give him the amount necessary for the service. There is such a thing as being too economical. The great question is to have the service as efficient as possible. From my own experience in the customs, while serving under the late government, I am led to believe that there are no drones in that service, that the men are all busy and that sometimes the importers have to wait an undue length of time before they can get their entries passed, because the staff is not sufficiently large to do the work within a reasonable time.

That is a good answer to the hon. minister.

Act. It is hoped that the fees for inspection will make good the deficiency. The expenditure last year was $7,168.93. We may perhaps be recouped the whole of this amount.
